nameStory: Dark columbine gets its name from its deep, dusky purple flowers that are so dark they appear almost black in certain light. The name 'columbine' comes from the Latin 'columba' meaning dove, because the flower's spurred petals were thought to resemble a cluster of doves drinking together.
description: Dark columbine is a rare perennial wildflower that's not native to New England but occasionally appears in specialized gardens or naturalized settings. This delicate plant grows 1-2 feet tall with distinctive nodding flowers that are deep purple to nearly black. Its compound leaves are divided into three-part leaflets that give it an airy, delicate appearance typical of columbines.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Deep purple to nearly black nodding flowers with five backward-pointing spurs that feel firm and waxy to touch, blooming in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Blue-green compound leaves divided into rounded, three-lobed leaflets that feel smooth and somewhat waxy, arranged alternately on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial herb growing 12-24 inches tall with slender, branching stems that feel slightly sticky when crushed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dry seed pods (follicles) that split open to release small black seeds, developing from the center of spent flowers

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, dark columbine is occasionally found in specialized rock gardens, alpine plant collections, or rarely naturalized in mountainous areas with well-drained, alkaline soils. When present, it prefers cool, moist conditions similar to its native Alpine habitat.

seasonality.spring: New blue-green foliage emerges in early spring, with distinctive three-part compound leaves unfurling from the base.
seasonality.summer: Dark purple to black flowers bloom in late spring to early summer, followed by developing seed pods through midsummer.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may turn yellow before dying back, and dried seed pods split open to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots, with no visible parts remaining above ground.

funFact: Dark columbine is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice according to naturalist records, making it one of the most elusive wildflowers in the region - you're more likely to see a moose than find this mysterious mountain beauty!
confusionNotes: The extremely dark flowers distinguish it from all other columbines in New England - red columbine has bright red and yellow flowers, while common columbine typically shows blue, purple, pink or white flowers, but never the distinctive near-black coloration of dark columbine.
contextualKnowledge: Dark columbine is native to European mountains (Alps and Apennines) and is not established in New England's flora. Any sightings are likely escaped garden plants or very temporary introductions, as our climate and soils don't match its native Alpine conditions.
compareHints: Dark columbine is easily separated from our native red columbine by its dark purple-black flowers versus red and yellow ones. Compared to the more common garden columbine, dark columbine's flowers are distinctively darker and more uniform in color, lacking the mixed colors or lighter shades typical of other columbine species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red columbine is the only native columbine species in New England, making it easy to distinguish from the escaped garden columbines you might occasionally find.
Common columbine can be distinguished from our native red columbine by its blue or purple flowers (versus bright red and yellow) and its more robust, bushier growth habit.
Blue columbine stands out from its eastern cousin, red columbine, primarily by color - blue and white versus red and yellow.
Golden columbine stands out from other columbines by its pure yellow flowers and extra-long spurs.
